You use the gerund at B2 level: the gerund of manner (llegó corriendo), of simultaneity (paseando por Triana, vimos…), of cause and condition (siendo tan tarde…, leyendo despacio…), the periphrases ir / venir / andar / llevar / seguir + gerund, and you avoid the typical mistakes (the gerund of posteriority and the gerund used as an adjective).
to have been… for some time (vengo diciendo)
Walking around Triana, we saw the bookshop.
My hand is getting better little by little.
My father had been keeping those books for years.
It being so late, we went to bed.
To use the gerund for the way an action is done: llegó corriendo, entró cantando.
To use the gerund for simultaneous actions, causes and conditions: paseando…, siendo tan tarde…, leyendo despacio…
To use the periphrases of duration and progression: ir, venir, andar, llevar, seguir + gerund.
To avoid the gerund of posteriority («Se cayó, rompiéndose la muñeca» ✗) and the gerund used as an adjective («una caja conteniendo libros» ✗).
To place pronouns correctly with the gerund: contándoselo, mirándola, sentándose.

Saturday, 25 April, morning, Seville. Pilar takes Ecaterina to the orange-tree courtyard of the hospital where she works, the one she promised her a year ago. Rosa Elena goes with them, with her camera.
Here it is. I’ve been coming to this courtyard to read for twenty years, always at the same time.
What a smell! Walking around Triana this morning I could already notice it, but here it’s something else.
Look, Ecaterina! A cat sleeping under the orange tree!
That’s Ramón. He’s been living here for years. We doctors take turns feeding him.
Your father used to talk to me about Seville. He said he got to know it doing his military service, in 1958.
Yes. And that he spent his Sundays reading in a bookshop in Triana. This afternoon you’re going to see it.
The one for the launch? I didn’t know. Andrés was always telling half-stories.
And your hand, how is it? Will you be able to sign this afternoon?
It’s getting better little by little. Signing slowly, I think so.
Done! I’ve taken a photo of you talking under the orange tree!
“llevo veinte años viniendo” = I’ve been coming for twenty years
“le vamos dando” = we take turns giving him
The stress always falls on “-AN-” or “-IEN-”: pa-se-AN-do, dur-MIEN-do, le-YEN-do. Verbs with a vowel before “-iendo” change it to “-yendo”: leer → leyendo, ir → yendo, oír → oyendo.
When you attach pronouns, the stress stays on the same syllable and is written: con-TAN-do → con-TÁN-do-se-lo, mi-RAN-do → mi-RÁN-do-la.
Stress on the second-to-last syllable: tri-A-na, na-RAN-ho. The “j” is aspirated, stronger than an English “h”.
1. The gerund of manner and of simultaneity
She came into the courtyard singing.
Walking around Triana, we saw the bookshop. (while)
I’ve taken a photo of you talking under the orange tree.
The Spanish gerund usually corresponds to the English -ing form. Where English uses “while…” or “-ing”, Spanish often uses the gerund.
2. The gerund of cause and of condition
It being so late, we went to bed. (cause)
Signing slowly, I think I’ll manage. (condition: if I sign slowly)
Reading every day, you learn an enormous amount. (condition)
action repeated for some time up to now
repeated action, with no clear direction (colloquial)
Andrés andaba contando historias a medias.
“Llevar + time + gerund” is very natural in Spanish and often replaces “hace… que”: «Llevo veinte años viniendo» = «Hace veinte años que vengo».
Se cayó y se rompió la muñeca.
the gerund doesn’t express a LATER action
Una caja que contenía libros. / con libros
the gerund is not an adjective
Te envío el libro adjuntando la foto.
Te envío el libro con la foto adjunta.
in letters, avoid the gerund as an adjective
Accepted exception: “agua hirviendo” (boiling water) and “una casa ardiendo” (a burning house) are used as adjectives.
¿Cuánto tiempo lleva Pilar viniendo al patio?

My father opened this bookshop in 1951, selling second-hand books on a wooden table. We have been opening every morning at ten for more than seventy years.
Poets, sailors, students and soldiers have passed through here one after another. Some came to read standing up, without buying anything, for years. My father never said a word to them.
One of those soldiers, a very thin madrileño, spent his Sundays sitting on the floor, reading poetry. Years later he opened his own bookshop in Madrid.
We go on selling books, even if it gets harder and harder. Coming through this door, you become part of the story. Remedios.

On 24 April, at nine in the morning, they left Atocha station on the high-speed train to Seville. There were four of them: Ecaterina, Ana, Rosa Elena and Marta. The others had gone back to Bucharest that same morning: Costel had to take a load to Bulgaria, and Señor Dan had promised to be home for his wife’s birthday. Mihai had stayed in Madrid with Andrei, because the two of them had decided, without explaining why, that they had to watch a football match together at the Bernabéu.

Rosa Elena spent the whole journey glued to the window, photographing everything that went by: olive trees, more olive trees, a castle on top of a hill, a flock of sheep, olive trees again. Crossing La Mancha, Ana pointed out some white windmills on the horizon and told her that a mad knight, in a very old book, had attacked them thinking they were giants. Rosa Elena looked at them for a long time and said she wasn’t surprised at all, because from far away they really did look like giants waving.

Marta sat opposite Ecaterina, the book open on her knees, but she wasn’t reading. She told her, looking out of the window, that her grandfather had talked about his military service in Seville only once, when she was twelve. He had told her it was the poorest and happiest year of his life, and that he had learnt to read poetry sitting on the floor of a bookshop, because he had no money to buy the books. Marta had never known which bookshop it was. Ecaterina told her that perhaps they would find out that afternoon. Marta looked at her in surprise. Ecaterina just smiled.

Pilar was waiting for them at Santa Justa station. It was twenty-eight degrees, although it was still April, and the air smelt of orange blossom in a way that seemed impossible. Ecaterina stood still at the station door, breathing deeply, with her eyes closed. Pilar explained that in April the whole of Seville smelt like that, that the orange trees in the streets all blossomed at once, and that some Sevillians went a little mad during those weeks. Ecaterina said she understood perfectly.

Pilar lived in Triana, in an old house near the river, with her husband, Manuel, who was a surgeon at the same hospital. She had a small courtyard with two orange trees, a fountain that didn’t work and a collection of flowerpots with geraniums. Manuel welcomed them at the door with an apron on and a frying pan in his hand, because he was frying fish for everyone. He kissed Ecaterina on both cheeks and told her he had been hearing about her for a year and could finally check whether everything Pilar said was true.

They had lunch in the courtyard, under the orange trees, with the sound of swallows flying in and out of the roofs. Manuel told hospital stories, roaring with laughter, and Rosa Elena showed him her photos from the train, explaining what everything was. Ana asked Pilar how they had met. Pilar told her it was on a Christmas Eve shift, twenty-five years ago, operating together on a man who had fallen off a roof trying to hang up his Christmas lights. Manuel added that the man had survived, and so had they.

In the living room, above the fireplace, Pilar had hung a new photo, in a silver frame: the 1972 photo the elderly gentleman had given her in Madrid, the one of her mother in the doorway of La Lámpara. Ecaterina went over to look at it. She was a young, dark-haired woman in a flowery dress, laughing. Ecaterina had never met her. She told Pilar that her mother looked very like her when she laughed. Pilar replied that her father always used to say that, and it was the first time in many years that anyone else had said it.

The next day, at nine, Pilar took Ecaterina and Rosa Elena to the hospital, to the orange-tree courtyard she had promised her a year earlier at Atocha station. It was a square courtyard, surrounded by arches, with eight orange trees in blossom and some stone benches. Pilar told her she had been coming there to read for twenty years, always at the same time, before starting her clinic. Rosa Elena immediately discovered a grey cat sleeping under one of the orange trees. Pilar told her it was called Ramón, and that the doctors took turns feeding it.

They sat down on a bench. Ecaterina took out of her bag the first letter Pilar had sent her, the hairdryer one, and read it again there, where it had been written. Then Pilar told her something she didn’t know: that her father had done his military service in Seville, in 1958, and spent his Sundays in a bookshop in Triana, reading standing up or sitting on the floor, because he had no money to buy anything. Ecaterina told her Andrés had talked to her about Seville, but always by halves, the way he told almost everything. Pilar smiled. She told her she would see it that afternoon.

After lunch, while Rosa Elena took her siesta in a hammock, Ecaterina and Marta went for a walk around Triana. They walked through narrow whitewashed streets, with flowerpots in every window and coloured tiles on the façades. In a little square, some children were playing football with a plastic ball, shouting in an Andalusian Spanish Ecaterina only half understood. They sat down on a bench in the shade. Marta told her she was thinking of writing another novel, and this time it wouldn’t be about her grandfather. Ecaterina asked her who it would be about. Marta answered: “About a bookseller in Triana who waits sixty years for an ending.” She didn’t yet know that such a person existed.

The bookshop in Triana was on a narrow street that ran down towards the river. It was tiny, with a low ceiling, walls covered in books to the top and a smell of old paper that mingled with the orange blossom from the street. By the door there was a wooden panel with the bookshop’s history handwritten on it. The owner, doña Remedios, was eighty-four and had inherited the bookshop from her father. She welcomed Ecaterina at the door, leaning on a stick just like hers, and told her she had been waiting for her since 1958.

Ecaterina didn’t understand. Doña Remedios explained, laughing, that she was sixteen when a very thin soldier from Madrid started coming on Sundays to read poetry sitting on the floor. Her father never said anything to him, although the soldier never bought anything. One Sunday, before going back to Madrid, the soldier gave her a handmade bookmark, with a lamp drawn on it, and told her that one day he would open a bookshop and keep the light on all the time. “I still have that bookmark,” said doña Remedios. “I’ve been waiting sixty-eight years for someone to tell me the ending.”

She took the bookmark out of a drawer in the counter. It was made of yellowed card, with worn edges, and it had a small, clumsy lamp drawn on it in ink, with shaky lines. Ecaterina took it carefully. She compared it, without saying anything, with the La Lámpara bookmark she had in her bag, the one she herself had designed in 1983, on a napkin. The two lamps were almost identical. Ecaterina realised then that in 1983, without knowing it, she had drawn the lamp Andrés had been imagining for twenty-five years.

Marta, who had heard the whole story standing by the door, came slowly over to the counter. Doña Remedios looked her up and down and asked whether she was the granddaughter. Marta said yes. Doña Remedios took her face in both hands, the way grandmothers do, and told her she had her grandfather’s eyes, the eyes of someone who reads standing up because they can’t wait to sit down. Marta burst out laughing and crying at the same time. She told her about the novel she had thought of that very afternoon, in the square. Doña Remedios told her she could write it, on one condition: that the ending be happy.

The launch began at seven, as the sun was starting to go down. Fifty people fitted in the bookshop, and eighty came, so half of them stayed in the street, fanning themselves with the publisher’s leaflets. One of doña Remedios’s grandsons played the guitar very softly in a corner. Ecaterina sat on a rush-seated chair, under a shelf of poetry, and read aloud the chapter about her first day at La Lámpara, the rainy day in 1977 when a bookseller offered her tea without asking her name. As she read, she realised her voice was shaking more than her hand.

Then Pilar spoke. She hadn’t prepared anything. She said that as a child she had hated that foreign woman who stole her father in the afternoons, and that it had taken her forty years to understand she hadn’t stolen anything: that her father, during those ten years, had been the happiest father in the world, and she had benefited from that happiness without knowing it. She said that now, reading the book, she had found the father she knew and another one she didn’t know, and she loved them both. Doña Remedios, in the front row, was drying her eyes with an embroidered handkerchief.

While Pilar was speaking, Rosa Elena had slipped out of Ana’s hands and sat down on the floor, among the audience’s legs, under a shelf, with a storybook open on her knees. She couldn’t read Spanish, but she turned the pages very seriously, looking at the pictures. Doña Remedios saw her and whispered to Ecaterina that that was exactly how the soldier from Madrid used to sit in 1958. Ecaterina looked at the little girl and couldn’t say anything. Andrei wasn’t there to take the photo, but Ana took it with her phone.

Then came the signing. Ecaterina’s hand was getting better day by day, and that afternoon she signed all eighty books without a break, faster than in Madrid. The Sevillians told her their stories out loud, unashamed, and laughed a lot. One lady told her she had met her husband in that very bookshop in 1965, both asking for the same book at the same time. A student asked her to sign the book “for my girlfriend, who lives in Bucharest and doesn’t know I’m going to go and find her”. Ecaterina wrote: “Go. And say goodbye properly if you ever have to leave.”

When they had finished, doña Remedios asked Ecaterina to sign two copies: one for her and another to put in the window, next to the 1958 bookmark, in a small glass case. In the first Ecaterina wrote: “For Remedios, who kept the first lamp.” In the second she wrote nothing. She said someone else had to sign that one, and gave it to Marta. Marta signed it under the title, with her grandfather’s name: “A. Gil”. The three of them stood looking at the book for a moment, without speaking.

Before they left, doña Remedios lent Ecaterina the 1958 bookmark, in an envelope, so that Andrei could photograph it in Madrid and make her a copy. She made her promise to bring it back in May, in person. Ecaterina asked her whether she wasn’t afraid to leave it with a stranger. Doña Remedios replied that she didn’t know her at all, but she had been waiting for her for sixty-eight years, and someone you’ve waited for that long can no longer be called a stranger.

After dark, they walked along the bank of the Guadalquivir. The Triana bridge was lit up, and the river reflected the lights on the other bank. Rosa Elena went ahead, photographing the bridge from every possible angle, because she had promised to send the photos to Señor Dan. Ana and Marta walked behind, talking about Andrei. Ecaterina and Pilar walked slowly, arm in arm, both with sticks. A small boat with music went by on the river. Pilar told Ecaterina she had one more thing to tell her, something she hadn’t told anyone.

She told her that when they cleared out the flat on the calle del Prado, after the funeral, she had found in the wardrobe in her father’s bedroom a shelf hidden behind the coats. On it were fourteen books in Romanian. They were novels by García Márquez, Cortázar, Vargas Llosa. All translated into Romanian by the same person: Ecaterina Ionescu. Her father didn’t know a word of Romanian. He had been buying them for years, nobody knew how, perhaps through some friend at the embassy, and keeping them there, in order, without showing them to anyone.

Ecaterina stopped in the middle of the promenade. She said nothing for a long time. The boat with the music had disappeared downriver. Then she asked, very quietly, whether the books had been read. Pilar told her they couldn’t be read, because they were in Romanian, but they all had worn pages, as if someone had opened them many times. And in each one, on the page with the translator’s name, there was a tiny pencil mark, barely visible: a lamp.

Pilar told her she had opened one of them at random, the night she found them, trying to understand something. It was “One Hundred Years of Solitude”, in Romanian. Between the pages there was a Madrid metro ticket from 1990 and a cutting from a Romanian newspaper with a small photo of Ecaterina at a book fair in Bucharest. Her father must have got hold of it somehow, perhaps through the same friend at the embassy. Pilar told her she had sat on the bedroom floor for an hour, with that photo in her hand, not knowing whether to laugh or cry, doing both.

Pilar told her she had them at home, in a box, and that they were hers. That her father had kept them for her, even if he didn’t know it. Ecaterina shook her head. She told her the books should stay in Seville, in Pilar’s living room, under the photo of her mother. That she already had the letter, Rayuela and Lola’s lamp in Bucharest. That she didn’t need any more proof. And that she liked the idea that, in a house in Triana, there were fourteen books nobody could read and everybody understood.

They walked home across the bridge. Manuel was waiting with dinner laid in the courtyard, under the orange trees, with candles on the table because the power had gone off in half of Triana. They had gazpacho, Spanish omelette and fried fish. Rosa Elena fell asleep on Ecaterina’s lap before dessert, with her camera in her hand. Ecaterina stayed very still so as not to wake her. It being so late, nobody suggested going to bed; they all stayed there, talking quietly, until the power came back, after one o’clock.

Before going to sleep, in the guest room, Ecaterina opened the window onto the courtyard. The orange trees were still, and the scent of blossom came in in waves, stronger and stronger, as if the night were releasing it little by little. She thought of the thin soldier sitting on the floor of a bookshop in Triana, in 1958, drawing a lamp on a piece of card. She thought that for him she didn’t yet exist back then, and that, even so, he was already waiting for her without knowing it. She fell asleep with the window open, feeling that, for the first time, she knew the beginning of the story.

The next day, on the train back to Madrid, Ecaterina spent the first hour looking out of the window without saying anything. Marta was reading “La lámpara encendida” for the fourth time, underlining sentences in pencil. Ana was asleep. Rosa Elena was counting orange trees on the station platforms, aloud, in Spanish, until she got tired at number one hundred and twelve. As they passed through La Mancha again, Ecaterina asked Marta to lend her the pencil. In the margin of her own copy, on the last page, she drew a small lamp.

Mihai and Andrei were waiting at Atocha, sunburnt after the match. Andrei had news: Inés had just called him. The first edition of “La lámpara encendida”, three thousand copies, had sold out in three days, between Madrid, Seville and bookshops all over Spain that had ordered it after reading Begoña’s report. The publisher was going to print a second edition. Inés wanted to know whether Ecaterina wanted to change anything. Ecaterina stood thinking in the middle of the platform.

Then she told Andrei to call Inés and tell her yes, she wanted to change one thing. Just one. On the acknowledgements page, at the end of the book, she wanted to add a line. Andrei asked her which. Ecaterina took out of her bag doña Remedios’s bookmark, which she had lent her so that Andrei could photograph it, and showed it to him. “Thanks to Remedios, of Triana,” she said, “who kept the first lamp for sixty-eight years, waiting for the ending.” Andrei typed it into his phone, word for word. And he photographed the bookmark right there, on the platform, in the afternoon light.
